related_resources.reason: The 1980 observational book based on studying New York City plazas. Whyte did not establish universal design laws.
Summarizes Whyte on sitting behavior, movable chairs, seating choices and amenities; guidance rather than a randomized effectiveness study.
Retrospective on Whyte’s Street Life Project, observational techniques and findings.
International age-friendly city guidance and context; the detailed design checklist is also characterized in the WHO launch release.
Reports consultation with older people in 33 cities in 22 countries and explicitly recommends well-located, maintained public benches and accessible toilets.
Notes armrests and backrests can aid older adults rising from seats, and suggests appropriate spacing, location and seating comfort; not experimental efficacy data.
Supports a variety of seating at accessible intervals, with room for mobility devices, varied sun/shade, and backrests or armrests for many users.
Describes benches/leaning bars for pedestrians and transit users and ways to suggest sites or report maintenance problems.
Explains plazas open to the public on private property in exchange for development benefits; the program began with 1961 zoning.
Current public plaza seating standards requiring multiple seating configurations and barring certain seat-inhibiting devices; regulation applies to specified plazas, not every public bench.
Public signage, amenity and complaint framework for privately owned public spaces; distinguishes formal access rights from actual usability.
Documents contested terminology of hostile and defensive design and argues for separate normative analysis of distinct cases.
Qualitative study based on interviews with 15 unhoused persons and reported experiences of exclusion and stress; not representative or causal evidence.
